answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439 (art. 12) left admission categories to the Executive. Its regulation, Decreto 1023/94, art. 15(b), gave residence to the parents, spouses, unmarried children under 21 and disabled children of permanent or temporary residents. I could not read the decree; its content is rebuilt from a 2006 DNM disposition that applies the same categories. Practice evidence is thin: a December 2003 Página/12 report quoting CELS says regularisation under the Ley Videla was blocked by red tape and costs above 2,500 pesos for a family of four.

Ley 25.871 was in force from 21 Jan 2004. Arts. 3(d) and 10 guarantee reunification with parents, spouses, unmarried minor children and disabled adult children; art. 22 makes relatives of Argentines permanent residents. Until Decreto 616/2010 the Decreto 1023/94 categories stayed applicable under art. 124, and DNM Disp. 48.328/2006 art. 13(b) still applies them to relatives of permanent residents. Practice: a blog citing figures says that in 2004 over 13,700 residence applications were filed and fewer than 3,000 resolved. This is thin, second-hand evidence.

The law was the same as in 2005. Decreto 616/2010 was published on 6 May 2010 and took effect 60 days later, so on this date the transitional Decreto 1023/94 categories still applied. Practice: the CMW 2011 concluding observations record mass regularisation (Patria Grande granted residence to more than half of 423,711 applicants). They raise no concern about family-based residence, but criticise the DNM for ignoring family ties when ordering expulsions.

Decreto 616/2010 was in force from July 2010. Art. 22(a)-(b) gives permanent residence to the spouse, parent, unmarried child under 18 or disabled adult child of Argentines and of permanent residents; the last paragraph of art. 23 gives temporary residence to the same relatives of temporary residents. This is the same regime the starting answer rests on; DNU 70/2017 later only narrowed the family-unity waiver in expulsion cases. I found no readable 2013-2016 practice source specific to family residence, so the rating carries forward from the 2010-2011 evidence.

answers.sourcing_note: I read the original and current texts of Ley 25.871 and Ley 22.439, and Decreto 616/2010, on InfoLEG and argentina.gob.ar. The Decreto 1023/94 text (an SCBA PDF) could not be opened, so its art. 15 is rebuilt from DNM Disp. 48.328/2006. Practice evidence before 2010 is thin and general, not specific to family residence.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The reunification objective is art. 3(d) of Ley 25.871, not 3(e). Temporary residents' relatives are covered by the last paragraph of Decreto 616 art. 23, not by an 'art. 23.N'. Neither point changes the answer.
answers.notes: No court decision is relied on; the protection rests on statutes and regulations only. Ley 26.202 (the Migrant Workers Convention) is cited through Decreto 616 art. 10; I did not open Ley 26.202 itself. The scope narrowed between 2000 and 2020: the age limit for children fell from under 21 (1023/94 era) to under 18 (Decreto 616). That narrowing, together with the 2004 statutory guarantee, is why I chose 'not the same' rather than a change in implementation only.

answers_by_date.basis: Under Ley 22.439, arts. 73-80, a refusal of admission or residence could be challenged only by administrative reconsideration and an appeal to the Ministry of the Interior, whose 'decisión ... causará ejecutoria, no existiendo ulterior recurso'. Judicial review was left only to the general constitutional amparo (CN art. 43, from 1994). Practice: CELS, quoted in the press in 2003, describes DNM decisions taken 'sin ningún control judicial'.

Ley 25.871 arts. 74 and 79-84 (in force 21 Jan 2004) provide administrative and judicial review when 'se deniegue la admisión o la permanencia'. Art. 82 gives appeals suspensive effect, and arts. 87-88 bar fees from blocking access to remedies. Practice: in Dec 2003 CELS warned the law could stay a dead letter until regulated, and that Decreto 322/95 still demanded a 300-peso fee to appeal. No later review of the 2004-2005 period could be read.

Same provisions as in 2005; Decreto 616/2010 left arts. 74-85 unregulated. Practice: the CMW in 2011 noted 'the rights of migrants to appeal decisions of the DNM'. It also noted that temporary permits are not extended while appeals are pending, which leaves appellants in irregular status.
Same provisions; DNU 70/2017 (in force 31 Jan 2017) came later and mainly changed expulsion procedure. No readable practice source for 2013-2016 was found, so the 2010-2011 rating carries forward.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

answers.sourcing_note: I read the original texts of Ley 22.439 and Ley 25.871. Ley 24.393 amended other articles of Ley 22.439; I did not open it, but art. 80 is shown unamended in the text I read. The IACHR De la Torre friendly settlement (Report 85/11) was blocked by Cloudflare, and CELS annual-report PDFs could not be converted.
answers.notes: I coded 2000 as 'Conditional' by analogy with the instrument's Colombia tutela example: the migration statute excluded any judicial appeal, and only the general amparo of CN art. 43 remained. No court decision is relied on. The 2017-2020 evidence (125 family-unity expulsion cases, 3-day appeal deadlines) concerns expulsions under DNU 70/2017, not refusals of reunification.

answers_by_date.basis: The family categories in Decreto 1023/94 and Ley 22.439 used 'cónyuge', which under the Civil Code then meant only a different-sex marriage. There was no national recognition of same-sex couples; the Buenos Aires City civil union of 2002-2003 is local and not part of the migration framework. No practice is relevant.
Ley 25.871 art. 10 and art. 22 refer to 'cónyuges'; marriage was still different-sex only, since Ley 26.618 did not yet exist.
Same as 2005. Ley 26.618 was enacted on 15 Jul 2010 and promulgated on 21 Jul 2010, after this date.

Since Ley 26.618 (July 2010), Civil Code art. 172 gives marriage the same requirements and effects regardless of sex. Art. 42 applies every legal reference to marriage to same-sex marriages too, so 'cónyuge' in Ley 25.871 art. 10 and Decreto 616 art. 22-23 includes same-sex spouses. I found no practice source for this period; the implementation rating carries over from the starting answer, with low confidence.

answers.change_2000_2020: There was no right protection (as of January 1, 2000), but there is now (as of January 1, 2020)

answers.repealed_search: For 2000-2010 I searched for any national recognition of same-sex partners in Ley 22.439, Decreto 1023/94 (as reflected in DNM Disp. 48.328/2006, which lists only 'padres, cónyuges, hijos'), Ley 25.871 and DNM dispositions. I found none before Ley 26.618, and no protection that existed and was later repealed.
answers.sourcing_note: I read Ley 26.618 on InfoLEG, but the page did not show the exact date it was published in the Boletín Oficial. I found no practice evidence on same-sex spouse residences for any period.
answers.notes: Protection follows from the general marriage-equality statute, Ley 26.618 art. 42, applied to Ley 25.871's 'cónyuges'. The implementation rating for 2015 has no practice evidence behind it.

answers_by_date.basis: I found no income, means or insurance condition for family-based residence in Ley 22.439. The family categories of Decreto 1023/94 art. 15 (rebuilt from later DNM rules) require only proof of the family tie and of the relative's residence; the decree itself could not be read. Practice: CELS in 2003 reported that procedure costs above 2,500 pesos for a family of four were a frequent barrier. These are fees, not a resource condition.

Ley 25.871 art. 10 and the original art. 22 impose no means requirement; the requirement to prove 'medios económicos suficientes' was added only by DNU 366/2025. DNM Disp. 48.328/2006 asks family applicants for documents proving the tie and the relative's residence, with no income test. Practice evidence is thin.

Same law as 2005. Decreto 616/2010 (in force July 2010) imposes means tests only on other categories such as rentistas, not on art. 22(a)-(b) or art. 23 family residence. Practice: the CMW 2011 observations raise no resource-based barrier to family residence; their concerns are fees and documentation.

Same provisions: Ley 25.871 arts. 10 and 22 (original) and Decreto 616 arts. 22-23, none with an income or insurance condition for family members. No specific practice source was found; the rating carries forward.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but the implementation level of these protections has changed
